comments.author: Alexander Terp
comments.body:
**Doctor found the app's daemon this time, which points at the first of the two causes this card asks between.** Measured 2026-09-01 while cutting 0.4.1.

    ./dev --doctor
      herdr daemons
        9 alive
        20747  09:12:22  /Users/amterp/.config/herdr/sessions/muster/herdr.sock  kept  6 pane(s) in ~/src/finances, ~/src, ~/src/spool, ...

So doctor does know where to look: `~/.config/herdr/sessions/muster/` is in the set it enumerates, and it marks the daemon `kept` rather than `scratch`. The second hypothesis - that it has never seen the app's daemon at all - is ruled out.

What is left is the first: the miss on 2026-08-31 was a daemon whose binary the upgrade had deleted out from under it. That is still the bug, and still the moment somebody reaches for pkill, but it is narrower than "doctor cannot see the app's daemon" - which is how the description currently reads. Worth rewording before anybody works on it.

The validation bullet about a replaced binary is the one that matters, and it is untested here: this daemon has been running 9h from a bundle nothing has touched since.

**Also: the contract tier's two daemons end cleanly, and by hand.** This run left `driving` and `problems` under /private/tmp/muster-smoke as usual (a_2I7ASgulK). Both ended with

    HERDR_SOCKET_PATH=<its socket> herdr server stop

which is the subcommand a_28YghIUw2 records as existing after all. No pkill, and the real daemon beside them was untouched - so whatever fixes a_2I7ASgulK has a graceful call available rather than needing to hunt pids.

creator: Alexander Terp
description:
`./dev --doctor` reported 11 herdr daemons and the app's own was not among them - the one process on the machine holding live agent sessions. That is the failure the tier exists to prevent: its own line says it "is what makes ending a stray daemon safe, since the process holding somebody's live agent looks exactly like the nineteen that hold nothing." Somebody reading that list would conclude every daemon on the machine was scratch and safe to end.

Measured 2026-08-31, immediately after upgrading the installed app to 0.4.0.

    ./dev --doctor
      herdr daemons
        11 alive
        14866  01:04  no API socket - a client rather than a daemon
        47952  ...    /private/tmp/muster-smoke/driving/config/herdr/sessions/muster/herdr.sock  scratch
        ... 9 more, all under /private/tmp/muster-smoke/

The missing one, found by asking who holds the socket instead:

    lsof ~/.config/herdr/sessions/muster/herdr.sock
    herdr  69388  ...  /Users/amterp/.config/herdr/sessions/muster/herdr.sock

    ps: 69388  Sun 30 Aug 17:42  /Applications/Muster.app/Contents/MacOS/herdr server

It held three panes with agents in them, including the session that ran the command.

Worth working out which of two it is before fixing, because the shape of the miss decides the fix. Either doctor matches on something that stopped being true when the app was replaced - the daemon had been running since the day before, from a path the upgrade deleted - or it enumerates from a set of known socket locations that has never included `~/.config/herdr/sessions/muster/`, in which case it has never seen the app's daemon at all and the scratch ones are all it has ever reported.

The second is worse and is cheap to tell apart: run it against a freshly started app on a machine with no scratch daemons and see whether the list comes back empty.

## A second thing the same run turned up

Ten of the eleven were left by `./dev --contract`, two per run (`driving` and `problems`), each holding one pane under `/private/tmp/muster-smoke/`. Doctor's own note says "the test harness tears its own daemons down; what accumulates is what a person or a fixture started outside it" - so the contract tier's app-launched daemons fall outside that teardown. Five runs in one session left ten behind. Harmless on their own (twenty together drew 0.1% CPU, a_28YghIUw2), and they are what made the real daemon hard to pick out.

## Validating a fix

- With an app running and agents in its panes, `./dev --doctor` names that daemon and says how many panes it holds.
- A daemon whose binary has been replaced on disk is still listed. That is the state a `brew upgrade` leaves behind, and it is exactly when somebody reaches for pkill.
- `./dev --contract` leaves no daemon behind, or doctor marks the ones it does as the contract tier's.
title: 🩺 doctor lists every daemon but the one holding live agents
